title: Sawatdi: one word for the whole day
title_target: สวัสดีครับ — Sà-wàt-dii khráp
goal: Greet people, ask how they are, say thank you, and say goodbye — while building the habit that shapes the rest of this course: the ครับ/ค่ะ tail.
bekal: greet anyone, any time of day, with สวัสดี
choose the ครับ or ค่ะ tail according to your own gender
say goodbye at two levels of familiarity

dialogs.title: บทสนทนา — In the office lobby, in the morning
dialogs.intro: Budi has just moved to Bangkok and meets Nok, a coworker, in the elevator. Notice just one thing for now: the last word out of each person's mouth is never the same.

lines.text: [ดิฉัน|Dì-chǎn][ชื่อ|chûue][นก|Nók][ค่ะ|khâ] [ยินดี|Yin-dii][ที่|thîi][ได้|dâai][รู้จัก|rúu-jàk][ค่ะ|khâ]

lines.text: [ยินดี|Yin-dii][ครับ|khráp] [ขอโทษ|Khǎaw-thôot][ครับ|khráp] [ผม|phǒm][พูด|phûut][ไทย|Thai][ได้|dâai][นิดหน่อย|nít-nàwy]

lines.text: [ขอบคุณ|Khàwp-khun][มาก|mâak][ครับ|khráp] [แล้ว|Láaeo][เจอ|joee][กัน|kan][ครับ|khráp]

lines.speaker: นก:
lines.text: [แล้ว|Láaeo][เจอ|joee][กัน|kan][ค่ะ|khâ]

notes: **สวัสดี works all day long.** There's no separate "good morning" and "good evening" as in English — this one word is used from dawn to midnight, both to say hello and to say goodbye. The word itself is actually a modern invention: a professor coined it in the 1930s from the Sanskrit word *svasti* (well-being), and the government spread it by radio.

**ครับ and ค่ะ depend on the GENDER OF THE SPEAKER, not the listener.** ⚠️ This is the number-one mistake learners make. Men always say *ครับ khráp*, no matter who they're talking to. Women always say *ค่ะ khâ*. When Budi talks to Nok, it's still *ครับ*; when Nok talks to Budi, it's still *ค่ะ*.

**Women have TWO forms.** For statements: *ค่ะ khâ* (falling tone). For questions: *คะ khá* (high tone). Look at the dialogue: Nok says *สบายดีค่ะ* but *แล้วคุณล่ะคะ*. Men don't have to deal with this — *ครับ* covers both.

**Leaving off ครับ/ค่ะ isn't a grammar mistake, it's a manners mistake.** The sentence is still correct and still understood, but it sounds like an order from someone who's angry. Attach it to every sentence until it comes out on its own. In very close conversation people do drop it — but that's a decision for later, not now.

**ผม and ดิฉัน both mean "I", and the choice also follows the speaker's gender.** Men: *ผม phǒm*. Women: *ดิฉัน dì-chǎn* (rather formal) or *ฉัน chǎn* (casual). In everyday chat many women use *เรา rao*, which here means "I", not "we".
**ก็ kâw means "also, too" and goes BEFORE the adjective**, not after: *ผมก็สบายดี* = "I'm fine too". You'll see this word throughout the course; it's one of the most frequent words in Thai.

**ไม่เป็นไร mâi pen rai is the phrase you'll hear most in Thailand.** Literally "not be anything", it does three jobs at once: "no problem", "you're welcome" (in reply to thanks), and "never mind, let it go". ⚠️ Note that it's often said even when something clearly is wrong — that's part of how Thailand keeps the atmosphere pleasant.

after: On the street, *ครับ* is often shortened to *ขับ khráp* with the *r* nearly gone, or even just *คับ kháp*. You don't need to copy that; say it in full and you'll sound polite, not stiff.

grammars.title: Four sentences that cover the first small talk
body: These four lines are a complete first introduction in Thai. Learn them as one block, not word by word.

head: Thai
Pronunciation
Meaning
rows: สวัสดีครับ/ค่ะ
สบายดีไหมครับ/คะ
สบายดีครับ/ค่ะ
ขอบคุณครับ/ค่ะ

after: ⚠️ *สบายดีไหม* isn't actually an automatic greeting like English "How are you?". Thais use it with people they **haven't seen for a while**. For people you see every day, the more natural greeting is *ไปไหนมา pai nǎi maa* ("where have you been?") or *กินข้าวหรือยัง kin khâao rǔue yang* ("have you eaten?") — both are small talk, not real questions.

sections.title: Thank you, sorry, and ไหว้

blocks.text: You'll use the words below dozens of times a day in Thailand. They always take the politeness tail.

head: Thai
Pronunciation
Meaning
When
rows: bumping into someone, interrupting, getting attention
in reply to thanks or an apology

blocks.title: ไหว้ — a greeting that isn't a word
items: *ไหว้ wâai* is the gesture of pressing both palms together in front of your chest while bowing your head slightly. It goes with *สวัสดี* and *ขอบคุณ*, and its height shows respect: the higher the fingertips, the more respect.

**The practical rule is simple:** the younger or lower-ranking person goes first; the older person returns it with lower hands. As a foreigner you won't be blamed whatever you do — but returning a *ไหว้* is always appreciated.
⚠️ One common mistake: **don't *ไหว้* waiters, cashiers, or staff** who are serving you. A nod and *ขอบคุณครับ/ค่ะ* is enough. A *ไหว้* to them actually makes things awkward.

head: Thai
Pronunciation
How it feels
rows: สวัสดีครับ/ค่ะ
แล้วเจอกัน
farewell — formal, sounds like a long parting

blocks.text: ⚠️ *ลาก่อน laa-kàwn* is often taught as "goodbye" in textbooks, but Thais rarely use it. It sounds heavy, like parting for a very long time. To leave a meeting room or a food stall, use *แล้วเจอกัน* or simply *สวัสดีครับ/ค่ะ*.
